question:
An object weighs 60 N when measured on the Earth. What would be its weight when measured on the moon?

(Given, acceleration due to gravity (g) of the moon is 1/6 th of the g of the earth)
solution:
The correct answer is __**10 N**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The weight of an object depends on the gravitational force acting on it, which varies from planet to planet.
 
• On the Earth, the object weighs 60 N due to Earth's gravitational acceleration (g ≈ 9.81 m/s²).
 
• The Moon's gravitational acceleration is approximately 1/6th that of Earth's (g ≈ 1.63 m/s²).
 
• Weight on the Moon is calculated by dividing the Earth's weight by 6 (60 N ÷ 6 = 10 N).
 
• Therefore, the object would weigh 10 N on the Moon.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gravitational Force:**

 
 
• It is the force that attracts a body towards the center of the Earth or any other celestial body.
 
• The gravitational force on the Moon is about 1/6th of that on Earth.
 
 
 
• **Weight vs. Mass:**
 
 
• Weight is the force exerted by gravity on an object (measured in Newtons).
 
• Mass is the amount of matter in an object (measured in kilograms) and remains constant regardless of location.
 
 
 
• **Newton's Second Law of Motion:**
 
 
• It states that the force acting on an object is equal to the mass of the object multiplied by its acceleration (F = ma).
 
• On the Moon, the acceleration due to gravity is less, hence the weight is less for the same mass.
 
 
 
• **Scientific Significance:**
 
 
• Understanding weight differences on different celestial bodies is crucial for space exploration and missions.
 
• Astronauts need to adjust for these differences during lunar missions.
